final_proof:
Let \(\mathcal F\) be the directed set of all finite subsets of \(\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}\), ordered by inclusion, and put \(a_n=\lVert v_n\rVert\). For \(F\in\mathcal F\), define \(t_F=\sum_{n\in F}a_n\), and for \(N\in\mathbb N\), define \(s_N=\sum_{n=1}^N a_n\). By the definitions of absolute net convergence and absolute convergence of a series, statement (1) says precisely that the net \((t_F)_{F\in\mathcal F}\) converges in \(\mathbb R\) to \(r\), while statement (2) says precisely that the sequence \((s_N)_{N\in\mathbb N}\) converges in \(\mathbb R\) to \(r\). Thus it remains to prove that these two modes of convergence are equivalent.

Assume (1), and let \(\varepsilon>0\). Since \(t_F\to r\), there is a finite set \(F_0\subseteq\mathbb N\) such that \(F\supseteq F_0\) implies \(|t_F-r|<\varepsilon\). Choose \(N_0\) so large that \(F_0\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N_0\}\). For every \(N\ge N_0\), the set \(I_N=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) contains \(F_0\), and hence
\[
\lvert s_N-r\rvert=\lvert t_{I_N}-r\rvert<\varepsilon.
\]
Therefore \(s_N\to r\), which is (2).

Conversely, assume (2). Because every \(a_n\ge0\), the sequence \((s_N)\) is nondecreasing. Moreover, \(s_m\le r\) for every \(m\): indeed, \(s_N\ge s_m\) for all \(N\ge m\), and passage to the limit gives \(r\ge s_m\). Let \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(N\) such that \(0\le r-s_N<\varepsilon\), and set \(F_0=I_N\). If \(F\in\mathcal F\) contains \(F_0\), choose \(M\) with \(F\subseteq I_M\). Nonnegativity of the \(a_n\)'s then gives
\[
s_N=t_{F_0}\le t_F\le s_M\le r.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\lvert t_F-r\rvert=r-t_F\le r-s_N<\varepsilon.
\]
This proves that \(t_F\to r\), which is (1). Hence (1) and (2) are equivalent. (The Banach-space hypothesis is not needed for this equivalence of the absolute scalar sums; it guarantees, in the usual accompanying theory, that finite total norm also yields convergence of the corresponding vector sums.)
